title: Accessible Media Players & Embedding 🖥️
description: Build or choose a video player with full keyboard control, captions, and screen reader support.

slides.title: The Native `<video>` Player Is Your Friend 🎥
slides.content:
HTML `<video controls>` provides built‑in accessibility:

* Keyboard operability (Tab to controls, Space/Enter to activate, arrow keys for seek/volume).
* Captions via `<track>`.
* Screen readers announce the video and controls.

However, native players have limitations (styling, feature gaps). If you build a custom player, you must replicate all accessibility.

quizData.question: Which of the following is true about the native `<video>` controls?

options.text: They are fully keyboard accessible in all modern browsers

quizData.explanation: Native controls meet WCAG keyboard requirements out of the box.

slides.title: Building a Custom Accessible Player 🛠️
slides.content:
A custom player must have:

* **Toggle buttons** for Play/Pause, Mute, Captions, Fullscreen – each with `aria-label` and `aria-pressed` or state management.
* **Slider** for seek bar and volume (use `role="slider"`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`, `aria-valuenow`).
* **Keyboard shortcuts**: Space for play/pause, Left/Right for seek, Up/Down for volume.
* **Focus management**: after interacting, focus should stay on the control.

Start with native `<video>` element, hide its controls, and build your own controls that interact with the video via JavaScript.

slides.title: Simple Custom Control Snippet
slides.codeSnippet:
<video id="my-video" src="movie.mp4" controls="false">
  <track kind="captions" src="movie.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
</video>
<button id="play-btn" aria-label="Play" aria-pressed="false">▶</button>

quizData.question: What attribute should a custom play button use to indicate its toggle state?
quizData.explanation: `aria-pressed='true'/'false'` communicates the toggle state of play/pause.

slides.title: Embedding Videos from Platforms (YouTube, Vimeo) 🎬
slides.content:
Embedded players from YouTube and Vimeo are partially accessible – they handle keyboard and captions but may have ARIA gaps.

* Always use the platform's embed code that includes `title` attribute on the iframe: `<iframe title="Video title">`.
* Ensure the video itself has proper captions (upload your own VTT if possible).
* Provide a text transcript alongside the embedded video.

Never embed a video in a way that auto‑plays with sound – this disturbs screen readers and violates WCAG.

quizData.question: What is the most important accessibility attribute for an `<iframe>` containing a video?
quizData.explanation: The `title` attribute provides an accessible name for the iframe, so screen reader users know what it contains.

slides.title: Accessible Media Player Libraries 📚
slides.content:
Consider using well‑tested accessible players:

* **AblePlayer** – fully accessible, supports captions, audio descriptions, transcripts.
* **Plyr** – modern, but check accessibility status.
* **Video.js** – with accessibility plugin.

Never reinvent the wheel if a mature, accessible player exists.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Test your player with a screen reader
Can you tell what each button does? Does the player announce the current time when seeking? Subtle announcements make a huge difference.
